at every state and action. Therefore every point in 𝒟⁡(D)\mathcal{D}(D) is generated by a policy in Π⁡(D)\Pi(D).

For any π∈Π⁡(D)\pi\in\Pi(D),

∑s,aρπ​(s,a)​r​(s,a)\displaystyle\sum_{s,a}\rho^{\pi}(s,a)r(s,a) =(1−γ)​∑t=0∞γt​∑s,aPrπ⁡(st=s,at=a)​r​(s,a)\displaystyle=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\sum_{s,a}\Pr^{\pi}(s_{t}=s,a_{t}=a)r(s,a)
=(1−γ)​∑t=0∞γt​𝔼π​[r⁡(st,at)]\displaystyle=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\mathbb{E}^{\pi}[r(s_{t},a_{t})]
=(1−γ)​∑t=0∞γt​𝔼π​[Rt]\displaystyle=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\mathbb{E}^{\pi}[R_{t}]
=(1−γ)​Vπ​(μ0).\displaystyle=(1-\gamma)V^{\pi}(\mu_{0}).

The third equality uses 𝔼[Rt∣st,at]=r(st,at)\mathbb{E}[R_{t}\mid s_{t},a_{t}]=r(s_{t},a_{t}) and the tower property. Steps 3 and 4 give a correspondence between supported policies and feasible occupancies, so maximizing the LP is equivalent to maximizing Vπ​(μ0)V^{\pi}(\mu_{0}) over Π⁡(D)\Pi(D). Its optimal value is therefore (1−γ)​VD∗​(μ0)(1-\gamma)V_{D}^{*}(\mu_{0}).

Summing the flow constraints over all states yields

∑s,aρ⁡(s,a)\displaystyle\sum_{s,a}\rho(s,a) =(1−γ)​∑sμ0​(s)\displaystyle=(1-\gamma)\sum_{s}\mu_{0}(s)
+γ∑s′,a′ρ(s′,a′)∑sP(s∣s′,a′)\displaystyle\quad+\gamma\sum_{s^{\prime},a^{\prime}}\rho(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\sum_{s}P(s\mid s^{\prime},a^{\prime})
=(1−γ)+γ​∑s′,a′ρ⁡(s′,a′).\displaystyle=(1-\gamma)+\gamma\sum_{s^{\prime},a^{\prime}}\rho(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}).

Therefore

∑s,aρ⁡(s,a)=1.\sum_{s,a}\rho(s,a)=1.

The set 𝒟⁡(D)\mathcal{D}(D) is defined by finitely many linear equalities, linear zero constraints, and nonnegativity constraints, so it is closed. The preceding identity and nonnegativity make it bounded. It is nonempty because any deterministic policy supported on DD has a feasible occupancy. Hence 𝒟⁡(D)\mathcal{D}(D) is compact, and the continuous linear objective attains its maximum.

It is enough to regard ρ⁡(s,a)\rho(s,a) for a∈D⁡(s)a\in D(s) as the primal variables. Associate an unrestricted dual variable v⁡(s)v(s) with each flow equality. The coefficient of a primal variable ρ⁡(x,a)\rho(x,a) in the equality indexed by ss is

𝟏{s=x}−γP(s∣x,a).\mathbf{1}\{s=x\}-\gamma P(s\mid x,a).

The corresponding dual inequality is

∑sv(s)[𝟏{s=x}−γP(s∣x,a)]≥r(x,a),\sum_{s}v(s)[\mathbf{1}\{s=x\}-\gamma P(s\mid x,a)]\geq r(x,a),

which is equivalent to

v⁡(x)≥r⁡(x,a)+γ​∑sP⁡(s∣x,a)​v​(s).v(x)\geq r(x,a)+\gamma\sum_{s}P(s\mid x,a)v(s).

This gives the dual in (54). The primal is feasible and bounded. The dual is feasible: the constant vector

v⁡(s)=11−γv(s)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}

satisfies, for every admissible action,

r⁡(s,a)+γ​∑s′P⁡(s′∣s,a)​v​(s′)≤1+γ1−γ=11−γ=v⁡(s).r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s^{\prime}}P(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)v(s^{\prime})\leq 1+\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}=v(s).

The finite-dimensional linear-programming strong-duality theorem therefore gives equality of the primal and dual optimal values.

Let 𝒪D\mathcal{O}_{D} be the set of primal optimizers. It is a nonempty closed subset of the compact set 𝒟⁡(D)\mathcal{D}(D) and is therefore compact. Order the n=|𝒮|​|𝒜|n=|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}| coordinates as 1,…,n1,\ldots,n. Set 𝒪D(0)=𝒪D\mathcal{O}_{D}^{(0)}=\mathcal{O}_{D}. For j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n, define

mj=minρ∈𝒪D(j−1)⁡ρj,𝒪D(j)={ρ∈𝒪D(j−1):ρj=mj}.m_{j}=\min_{\rho\in\mathcal{O}_{D}^{(j-1)}}\rho_{j},\qquad\mathcal{O}_{D}^{(j)}=\{\rho\in\mathcal{O}_{D}^{(j-1)}:\rho_{j}=m_{j}\}.

Each minimum is attained because 𝒪D(j−1)\mathcal{O}_{D}^{(j-1)} is nonempty and compact, so each 𝒪D(j)\mathcal{O}_{D}^{(j)} is again nonempty and compact. At the last step all coordinates are fixed, so 𝒪D(n)\mathcal{O}_{D}^{(n)} contains exactly one vector. This vector is the lexicographically smallest optimal occupancy and is denoted ρDlex\rho_{D}^{\mathrm{lex}}.

Finally, reconstruct a policy from ρDlex\rho_{D}^{\mathrm{lex}}, using the first action in D⁡(s)D(s) at every state with zero occupancy. The reconstructed policy has occupancy ρDlex\rho_{D}^{\mathrm{lex}} and attains the restricted optimal value. This supplies the unique response convention needed to evaluate the outer objective. ∎

Proof of Proposition C.2.

Fix θ\theta. Because 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒜\mathcal{A} are finite, the collection of score values

{gθ(s,a):s∈𝒮,a∈𝒜}\{g_{\theta}(s,a):s\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A}\}

is finite. As τ\tau varies, a raw set changes only when τ\tau crosses one of these values. The fallback action is also fixed by θ\theta and the tie-breaking order. Hence only finitely many complete raw–operational designs G=(Cθ,τ,Dθ,τ)G=(C_{\theta,\tau},D_{\theta,\tau}) can be induced by thresholds.

For any induced design, the lower occupancy LP depends only on DD. The lexicographic construction in Theorem C.1 therefore fixes one optimal occupancy and makes both the objective and coverage constraint functions of GG alone. The feasible induced designs form a finite set, so the objective attains its minimum whenever this set is nonempty.

It remains to prove nonemptiness. Since every score is finite, choose

τall≥maxs,a⁡gθ​(s,a).\tau_{\mathrm{all}}\geq\max_{s,a}g_{\theta}(s,a).

Then Cθ,τall​(s)=Dθ,τall​(s)=𝒜C_{\theta,\tau_{\mathrm{all}}}(s)=D_{\theta,\tau_{\mathrm{all}}}(s)=\mathcal{A} for every state. The oracle target is nonempty, so the retention probability equals one. Thus τall\tau_{\mathrm{all}} is feasible, and a minimizing threshold exists. ∎

D.3 Proof of the Quantile Characterization

The argument has two parts. The margin equivalence identifies the feasible thresholds, and nesting of the execution sets establishes size minimality under the same fixed occupancy.

Proof of Proposition C.3.

Fix θ\theta and π\pi. For every state ss,

Cθ,τ​(s)∩𝒜ε∗​(s)≠∅\displaystyle C_{\theta,\tau}(s)\cap\mathcal{A}^{*}_{\varepsilon}(s)\neq\emptyset
⟺there exists ​a∈𝒜ε∗​(s)​ with ​gθ​(s,a)≤τ\displaystyle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\text{there exists }a\in\mathcal{A}^{*}_{\varepsilon}(s)\text{ with }g_{\theta}(s,a)\leq\tau
⟺mina∈𝒜ε∗​(s)⁡gθ​(s,a)≤τ\displaystyle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\min_{a\in\mathcal{A}^{*}_{\varepsilon}(s)}g_{\theta}(s,a)\leq\tau
⟺mθ​(s)≤τ.\displaystyle\quad\Longleftrightarrow m_{\theta}(s)\leq\tau.

The minimum is well-defined because 𝒜ε∗​(s)\mathcal{A}^{*}_{\varepsilon}(s) is finite and nonempty. Taking probability under s∼dπs\sim d^{\pi} gives

Prs∼dπ⁡(Cθ,τ​(s)∩𝒜ε∗​(s)≠∅)=Fθ,π​(τ).\Pr_{s\sim d^{\pi}}\left(C_{\theta,\tau}(s)\cap\mathcal{A}^{*}_{\varepsilon}(s)\neq\emptyset\right)=F_{\theta,\pi}(\tau).

Thus τ\tau satisfies the coverage requirement if and only if

Fθ,π​(τ)≥1−α.F_{\theta,\pi}(\tau)\geq 1-\alpha.

Let

q=Fθ,π−1​(1−α)=inf{x:Fθ,π​(x)≥1−α}.q=F^{-1}_{\theta,\pi}(1-\alpha)=\inf\{x:F_{\theta,\pi}(x)\geq 1-\alpha\}.

Because 𝒮\mathcal{S} is finite, the random variable mθ​(s)m_{\theta}(s) has finite support under dπd^{\pi}. Hence its CDF is a right-continuous step function and the set

{x:Fθ,π​(x)≥1−α}\{x:F_{\theta,\pi}(x)\geq 1-\alpha\}

has a smallest element. That element is qq, so Fθ,π​(q)≥1−αF_{\theta,\pi}(q)\geq 1-\alpha. If τ<q\tau<q, then by the definition of the infimum and the fact that qq is the smallest feasible support point,

Fθ,π​(τ)<1−α.F_{\theta,\pi}(\tau)<1-\alpha.

If τ≥q\tau\geq q, monotonicity of the CDF gives

Fθ,π​(τ)≥Fθ,π​(q)≥1−α.F_{\theta,\pi}(\tau)\geq F_{\theta,\pi}(q)\geq 1-\alpha.

Therefore the feasible thresholds are exactly the interval [q,∞)[q,\infty), and the smallest feasible threshold is q=τmin​(θ,π)q=\tau_{\min}(\theta,\pi).

It remains to prove the set-size minimality under the same fixed policy. Let τ1≤τ2\tau_{1}\leq\tau_{2}. The raw sets are nested:

Cθ,τ1​(s)⊆Cθ,τ2​(s)for every ​s.C_{\theta,\tau_{1}}(s)\subseteq C_{\theta,\tau_{2}}(s)\qquad\text{for every }s.

We now verify that the operational sets are also nested.

If Cθ,τ1​(s)≠∅C_{\theta,\tau_{1}}(s)\neq\emptyset, then both operational sets equal their raw sets and

C¯θ,τ1​(s)=Cθ,τ1​(s)⊆Cθ,τ2​(s)=C¯θ,τ2​(s).\overline{C}_{\theta,\tau_{1}}(s)=C_{\theta,\tau_{1}}(s)\subseteq C_{\theta,\tau_{2}}(s)=\overline{C}_{\theta,\tau_{2}}(s).

If Cθ,τ1​(s)=∅C_{\theta,\tau_{1}}(s)=\emptyset and Cθ,τ2​(s)=∅C_{\theta,\tau_{2}}(s)=\emptyset, then both operational sets equal the same singleton {aθmin​(s)}\{a_{\theta}^{\min}(s)\}. Finally, suppose Cθ,τ1​(s)=∅C_{\theta,\tau_{1}}(s)=\emptyset but Cθ,τ2​(s)≠∅C_{\theta,\tau_{2}}(s)\neq\emptyset. Nonemptiness of the latter implies

τ2≥mina⁡gθ​(s,a)=gθ​(s,aθmin​(s)),\tau_{2}\geq\min_{a}g_{\theta}(s,a)=g_{\theta}(s,a_{\theta}^{\min}(s)),

so aθmin​(s)∈Cθ,τ2​(s)a_{\theta}^{\min}(s)\in C_{\theta,\tau_{2}}(s). Hence

C¯θ,τ1​(s)={aθmin​(s)}⊆Cθ,τ2​(s)=C¯θ,τ2​(s).\overline{C}_{\theta,\tau_{1}}(s)=\{a_{\theta}^{\min}(s)\}\subseteq C_{\theta,\tau_{2}}(s)=\overline{C}_{\theta,\tau_{2}}(s).

Thus

|C¯θ,τ1​(s)|≤|C¯θ,τ2​(s)||\overline{C}_{\theta,\tau_{1}}(s)|\leq|\overline{C}_{\theta,\tau_{2}}(s)|

for every state. Averaging with respect to the fixed distribution dπd^{\pi} preserves the inequality. Since every coverage-valid threshold is at least τmin​(θ,π)\tau_{\min}(\theta,\pi), that threshold minimizes the expected operational-set size among all thresholds evaluated under the same fixed policy. ∎

D.4 Proof of Pathwise Calibration

The update cannot move arbitrarily far beyond the realized margin range: outside that range, its direction points back toward it. We first formalize this interval bound and then express the cumulative calibration error in terms of threshold increments.

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

Fix an arbitrary horizon T≥1T\geq 1 and define

m¯T\displaystyle\underline{m}_{T} =min⁡{τ1,m1,…,mT},\displaystyle=\min\{\tau_{1},m_{1},\ldots,m_{T}\},
m¯T\displaystyle\overline{m}_{T} =max⁡{τ1,m1,…,mT}.\displaystyle=\max\{\tau_{1},m_{1},\ldots,m_{T}\}.

Then WT=m¯T−m¯TW_{T}=\overline{m}_{T}-\underline{m}_{T}. Define

τT−=m¯T−α​η1,τT+=m¯T+(1−α)​η1.\tau_{T}^{-}=\underline{m}_{T}-\alpha\eta_{1},\qquad\tau_{T}^{+}=\overline{m}_{T}+(1-\alpha)\eta_{1}.

τt∈[τT−,τT+]for every ​1≤t≤T+1.\tau_{t}\in[\tau_{T}^{-},\tau_{T}^{+}]\qquad\text{for every }1\leq t\leq T+1. (55)

The base case holds because τ1∈[m¯T,m¯T]\tau_{1}\in[\underline{m}_{T},\overline{m}_{T}]. Assume the claim holds for some t≤Tt\leq T. Since ηt≤η1\eta_{t}\leq\eta_{1}, there are three cases.

If τt<m¯T\tau_{t}<\underline{m}_{T}, then mt≥m¯T>τtm_{t}\geq\underline{m}_{T}>\tau_{t}, so et=1e_{t}=1 and

τt+1=τt+(1−α)​ηt.\tau_{t+1}=\tau_{t}+(1-\alpha)\eta_{t}.

The update is nonnegative, so τt+1≥τt≥τT−\tau_{t+1}\geq\tau_{t}\geq\tau_{T}^{-}. Also,

τt+1\displaystyle\tau_{t+1} <m¯T+(1−α)​ηt\displaystyle<\underline{m}_{T}+(1-\alpha)\eta_{t}
≤m¯T+(1−α)​η1=τT+.\displaystyle\leq\overline{m}_{T}+(1-\alpha)\eta_{1}=\tau_{T}^{+}.

If m¯T≤τt≤m¯T\underline{m}_{T}\leq\tau_{t}\leq\overline{m}_{T}, then et∈{0,1}e_{t}\in\{0,1\} and

τt−α​ηt≤τt+1≤τt+(1−α)​ηt.\tau_{t}-\alpha\eta_{t}\leq\tau_{t+1}\leq\tau_{t}+(1-\alpha)\eta_{t}.

Using ηt≤η1\eta_{t}\leq\eta_{1} and the bounds on τt\tau_{t} yields τT−≤τt+1≤τT+\tau_{T}^{-}\leq\tau_{t+1}\leq\tau_{T}^{+}.

If τt>m¯T\tau_{t}>\overline{m}_{T}, then mt≤m¯T<τtm_{t}\leq\overline{m}_{T}<\tau_{t}, so et=0e_{t}=0 and

τt+1=τt−α​ηt.\tau_{t+1}=\tau_{t}-\alpha\eta_{t}.

The update is nonpositive, so τt+1≤τt≤τT+\tau_{t+1}\leq\tau_{t}\leq\tau_{T}^{+}. Moreover,

τt+1\displaystyle\tau_{t+1} >m¯T−α​ηt\displaystyle>\overline{m}_{T}-\alpha\eta_{t}
≥m¯T−α​η1=τT−.\displaystyle\geq\underline{m}_{T}-\alpha\eta_{1}=\tau_{T}^{-}.

This completes the induction. The invariant interval has width

τT+−τT−\displaystyle\tau_{T}^{+}-\tau_{T}^{-} =(m¯T−m¯T)+η1\displaystyle=(\overline{m}_{T}-\underline{m}_{T})+\eta_{1} (56)
=WT+η1.\displaystyle=W_{T}+\eta_{1}.

The interval bound now controls the accumulated misses. Rearranging (12) gives

et−α=τt+1−τtηt.e_{t}-\alpha=\frac{\tau_{t+1}-\tau_{t}}{\eta_{t}}.

Let ct=1/ηtc_{t}=1/\eta_{t}. Because ηt\eta_{t} is positive and nonincreasing, ctc_{t} is positive and nondecreasing. Therefore

=∑t=1Tct​(τt+1−τt)\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}(\tau_{t+1}-\tau_{t})
=cT​τT+1−c1​τ1−∑t=2T(ct−ct−1)​τt.\displaystyle=c_{T}\tau_{T+1}-c_{1}\tau_{1}-\sum_{t=2}^{T}(c_{t}-c_{t-1})\tau_{t}.

ω1=c1cT,ωt=ct−ct−1cT(2≤t≤T).\omega_{1}=\frac{c_{1}}{c_{T}},\qquad\omega_{t}=\frac{c_{t}-c_{t-1}}{c_{T}}\quad(2\leq t\leq T).

D.5 Proofs for the Value Results

We begin with the counterexample separating retention from selection, then derive the exact value identity. The subsequent proofs bound its filtering and selection terms in turn, before combining them along an adaptive finite session.

Proof of Proposition C.4.

Consider one state ss, two actions ag,aba_{g},a_{b}, deterministic self-transitions, and rewards

r⁡(s,ag)=1,r⁡(s,ab)=0.r(s,a_{g})=1,\qquad r(s,a_{b})=0.

The optimal policy always chooses aga_{g}, so

V∗​(s)=∑t=0∞γt=11−γ.V^{*}(s)=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}.

The optimal action values are

Q∗​(s,ag)\displaystyle Q^{*}(s,a_{g}) =1+γ​V∗​(s)=11−γ,\displaystyle=1+\gamma V^{*}(s)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma},
Q∗​(s,ab)\displaystyle Q^{*}(s,a_{b}) =γ​V∗​(s)=γ1−γ.\displaystyle=\gamma V^{*}(s)=\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}.

Therefore 𝒜0∗​(s)={ag}\mathcal{A}^{*}_{0}(s)=\{a_{g}\}. Let D⁡(s)={ag,ab}D(s)=\{a_{g},a_{b}\}, so the set contains an optimal action with probability one. Let πb\pi_{b} always choose aba_{b}. This policy belongs to Π⁡(D)\Pi(D) and receives zero reward at every time, hence Vπb​(s)=0V^{\pi_{b}}(s)=0. Its value gap is

V∗​(s)−Vπb​(s)=11−γ.V^{*}(s)-V^{\pi_{b}}(s)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}.

Lemma D.2 shows that no value gap can be larger, so the gap is maximal. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.2.

We first verify that both terms are losses, then express their sum as the optimal Bellman residual of the supported policy. Since D⁡(s)D(s) is nonempty and V∗​(s)=maxa∈𝒜⁡Q∗​(s,a)V^{*}(s)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q^{*}(s,a),

maxa∈D⁡(s)⁡Q∗​(s,a)≤V∗​(s),\max_{a\in D(s)}Q^{*}(s,a)\leq V^{*}(s),

so ΔD​(s)≥0\Delta_{D}(s)\geq 0. Also, an average cannot exceed the maximum of the averaged numbers:

∑a∈D⁡(s)π⁡(a∣s)​Q∗​(s,a)≤maxa∈D⁡(s)⁡Q∗​(s,a),\sum_{a\in D(s)}\pi(a\mid s)Q^{*}(s,a)\leq\max_{a\in D(s)}Q^{*}(s,a),

so ζπ,D​(s)≥0\zeta_{\pi,D}(s)\geq 0.

Define the policy-averaged reward and transition kernel

rπ​(s)\displaystyle r^{\pi}(s) =∑aπ⁡(a∣s)​r​(s,a),\displaystyle=\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid s)r(s,a),
Pπ​(s′∣s)\displaystyle P^{\pi}(s^{\prime}\mid s) =∑aπ⁡(a∣s)​P​(s′∣s,a).\displaystyle=\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid s)P(s^{\prime}\mid s,a).

For any function ff on 𝒮\mathcal{S}, let

(Pπ​f)​(s)=∑s′Pπ​(s′∣s)​f​(s′).(P^{\pi}f)(s)=\sum_{s^{\prime}}P^{\pi}(s^{\prime}\mid s)f(s^{\prime}).

To relate these local gaps to the total value loss, define the optimal Bellman residual of π\pi by

bπ​(s)=V∗​(s)−∑aπ⁡(a∣s)​Q∗​(s,a).b_{\pi}(s)=V^{*}(s)-\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid s)Q^{*}(s,a).

Using (51),

∑aπ⁡(a∣s)​Q∗​(s,a)\displaystyle\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid s)Q^{*}(s,a)
=∑aπ⁡(a∣s)​r​(s,a)\displaystyle\quad=\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid s)r(s,a)
+γ∑s′[∑aπ(a∣s)P(s′∣s,a)]V∗(s′)\displaystyle\qquad+\gamma\sum_{s^{\prime}}\left[\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid s)P(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)\right]V^{*}(s^{\prime})
=rπ​(s)+γ⁡(Pπ​V∗)​(s).\displaystyle\quad=r^{\pi}(s)+\gamma(P^{\pi}V^{*})(s).

Lemma D.1 gives Vπ=rπ+γ​Pπ​VπV^{\pi}=r^{\pi}+\gamma P^{\pi}V^{\pi}. Subtracting this identity from V∗V^{*} yields, state by state,

V∗−Vπ\displaystyle V^{*}-V^{\pi} =V∗−rπ−γ​Pπ​Vπ\displaystyle=V^{*}-r^{\pi}-\gamma P^{\pi}V^{\pi}
=[V∗−rπ−γ​Pπ​V∗]+γ​Pπ​(V∗−Vπ)\displaystyle=\left[V^{*}-r^{\pi}-\gamma P^{\pi}V^{*}\right]+\gamma P^{\pi}(V^{*}-V^{\pi})
=bπ+γ​Pπ​(V∗−Vπ).\displaystyle=b_{\pi}+\gamma P^{\pi}(V^{*}-V^{\pi}).

Iterating this equality NN times gives

V∗−Vπ=\displaystyle V^{*}-V^{\pi}={} ∑t=0N−1γt​(Pπ)t​bπ\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{N-1}\gamma^{t}(P^{\pi})^{t}b_{\pi}
+γN​(Pπ)N​(V∗−Vπ).\displaystyle+\gamma^{N}(P^{\pi})^{N}(V^{*}-V^{\pi}).

‖γN​(Pπ)N​(V∗−Vπ)‖∞≤γN1−γ⟶0.\left\|\gamma^{N}(P^{\pi})^{N}(V^{*}-V^{\pi})\right\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\gamma^{N}}{1-\gamma}\longrightarrow 0.

V∗−Vπ=∑t=0∞γt​(Pπ)t​bπ.V^{*}-V^{\pi}=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}(P^{\pi})^{t}b_{\pi}.

Average both sides over s0∼μ0s_{0}\sim\mu_{0}. The definition (3) implies

V∗​(μ0)−Vπ​(μ0)\displaystyle V^{*}(\mu_{0})-V^{\pi}(\mu_{0}) =∑t=0∞γt​𝔼π​[bπ​(st)]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\mathbb{E}^{\pi}[b_{\pi}(s_{t})]
=11−γ​𝔼s∼dπ​[bπ​(s)].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\pi}}[b_{\pi}(s)].

Because π∈Π⁡(D)\pi\in\Pi(D),

bπ​(s)\displaystyle b_{\pi}(s) =V∗​(s)−∑a∈D⁡(s)π⁡(a∣s)​Q∗​(s,a)\displaystyle=V^{*}(s)-\sum_{a\in D(s)}\pi(a\mid s)Q^{*}(s,a)
=V∗​(s)−maxa∈D⁡(s)⁡Q∗​(s,a)\displaystyle=V^{*}(s)-\max_{a\in D(s)}Q^{*}(s,a)
+maxa∈D⁡(s)⁡Q∗​(s,a)−∑a∈D⁡(s)π⁡(a∣s)​Q∗​(s,a)\displaystyle\quad+\max_{a\in D(s)}Q^{*}(s,a)-\sum_{a\in D(s)}\pi(a\mid s)Q^{*}(s,a)
=ΔD​(s)+ζπ,D​(s).\displaystyle=\Delta_{D}(s)+\zeta_{\pi,D}(s).

Substitution proves (18). The decomposition is exact because it splits the same Bellman residual, rather than bounding filtering and selection through separate trajectory comparisons. ∎

Proof of Corollary C.5.

Define the hit set

H={s:C⁡(s)∩𝒜ε∗​(s)≠∅}H=\{s:C(s)\cap\mathcal{A}^{*}_{\varepsilon}(s)\neq\emptyset\}

and its miss probability under the policy occupancy:

απ=Prs∼dπ⁡(s∉H).\alpha_{\pi}=\Pr_{s\sim d^{\pi}}(s\notin H).

Assumption (31) gives

απ≤α.\alpha_{\pi}\leq\alpha.

Fix a state s∈Hs\in H. By definition of HH, there exists at least one action

aH​(s)∈C⁡(s)∩𝒜ε∗​(s).a_{H}(s)\in C(s)\cap\mathcal{A}^{*}_{\varepsilon}(s).

Since C⁡(s)⊆D⁡(s)C(s)\subseteq D(s),

aH​(s)∈D​(s).a_{H}(s)\in D(s).

Therefore

maxa∈D⁡(s)⁡Q∗​(s,a)\displaystyle\max_{a\in D(s)}Q^{*}(s,a) ≥Q∗​(s,aH​(s))\displaystyle\geq Q^{*}(s,a_{H}(s))
≥V∗​(s)−ε,\displaystyle\geq V^{*}(s)-\varepsilon,

where the second inequality follows from aH​(s)∈𝒜ε∗​(s)a_{H}(s)\in\mathcal{A}^{*}_{\varepsilon}(s). Rearranging gives

ΔD​(s)=V∗​(s)−maxa∈D⁡(s)⁡Q∗​(s,a)≤ε.\Delta_{D}(s)=V^{*}(s)-\max_{a\in D(s)}Q^{*}(s,a)\leq\varepsilon.

By definition of Δmax\Delta_{\max}, every nonempty set D⁡(s)D(s) also satisfies

0≤ΔD​(s)≤Δmax.0\leq\Delta_{D}(s)\leq\Delta_{\max}.

Hence, on the hit set,

ΔD​(s)≤min⁡{ε,Δmax}=ε0,\Delta_{D}(s)\leq\min\{\varepsilon,\Delta_{\max}\}=\varepsilon_{0},

while on the miss set,

ΔD​(s)≤Δmax.\Delta_{D}(s)\leq\Delta_{\max}.

Split the occupancy expectation over HH and its complement:

𝔼s∼dπ​[ΔD​(s)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\pi}}[\Delta_{D}(s)] =𝔼[ΔD(s)𝟏{s∈H}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{D}(s)\mathbf{1}\{s\in H\}]
+𝔼[ΔD(s)𝟏{s∉H}]\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{D}(s)\mathbf{1}\{s\notin H\}]
≤ε0​Pr⁡(s∈H)+Δmax​Pr⁡(s∉H)\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon_{0}\Pr(s\in H)+\Delta_{\max}\Pr(s\notin H)
=(1−απ)​ε0+απ​Δmax\displaystyle=(1-\alpha_{\pi})\varepsilon_{0}+\alpha_{\pi}\Delta_{\max}
=ε0+απ​(Δmax−ε0).\displaystyle=\varepsilon_{0}+\alpha_{\pi}(\Delta_{\max}-\varepsilon_{0}).

Since Δmax−ε0≥0\Delta_{\max}-\varepsilon_{0}\geq 0 and απ≤α\alpha_{\pi}\leq\alpha,

𝔼dπ​[ΔD​(s)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{d^{\pi}}[\Delta_{D}(s)] ≤ε0+α⁡(Δmax−ε0)\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon_{0}+\alpha(\Delta_{\max}-\varepsilon_{0})
=(1−α)​ε0+α​Δmax.\displaystyle=(1-\alpha)\varepsilon_{0}+\alpha\Delta_{\max}.

The exact decomposition in Theorem 3.2 gives

V∗​(μ0)−Vπ​(μ0)=𝔼dπ​[ΔD​(s)]+ζ¯π,D1−γ.V^{*}(\mu_{0})-V^{\pi}(\mu_{0})=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{d^{\pi}}[\Delta_{D}(s)]+\overline{\zeta}_{\pi,D}}{1-\gamma}.

Substituting the preceding bound proves (32). ∎

Proof of Corollary C.6.

Feasibility of (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau) in Problem (11) gives

Prs∼dπθ,τ∗⁡(Cθ,τ​(s)∩𝒜ε∗​(s)≠∅)≥1−α.\Pr_{s\sim d^{\pi^{*}_{\theta,\tau}}}\left(C_{\theta,\tau}(s)\cap\mathcal{A}^{*}_{\varepsilon}(s)\neq\emptyset\right)\geq 1-\alpha.

By construction,

Cθ,τ​(s)⊆Dθ,τ​(s)C_{\theta,\tau}(s)\subseteq D_{\theta,\tau}(s)

and Dθ,τ​(s)D_{\theta,\tau}(s) is nonempty for every state. The lower-level policy satisfies

πθ,τ∗∈Π⁡(Dθ,τ).\pi^{*}_{\theta,\tau}\in\Pi(D_{\theta,\tau}).

Thus every assumption of Corollary C.5 holds after setting

C=Cθ,τ,D=Dθ,τ,π=πθ,τ∗.C=C_{\theta,\tau},\qquad D=D_{\theta,\tau},\qquad\pi=\pi^{*}_{\theta,\tau}.

The stated bound follows directly. ∎

The occupancy bound concerns retention averaged under a specified policy. Under the stronger condition that every state retains a target action, we can instead compare the restricted and unrestricted optimal values at every initial state.

Corollary D.3 (Pointwise retention).

If D⁡(s)∩𝒜ε∗​(s)≠∅D(s)\cap\mathcal{A}^{*}_{\varepsilon}(s)\neq\emptyset for every state, then

0≤V∗​(s)−VD∗​(s)≤ε01−γ∀s.0\leq V^{*}(s)-V_{D}^{*}(s)\leq\frac{\varepsilon_{0}}{1-\gamma}\qquad\forall s. (57)
Proof of Corollary D.3.

For every state ss, choose

aQ​(s)∈arg​maxa∈D⁡(s)⁡Q∗​(s,a)a_{Q}(s)\in\argmax_{a\in D(s)}Q^{*}(s,a)

using a fixed tie-breaking rule, and let πQ\pi_{Q} be the deterministic policy that selects aQ​(s)a_{Q}(s). Because aQ​(s)∈D​(s)a_{Q}(s)\in D(s),

πQ∈Π⁡(D).\pi_{Q}\in\Pi(D).

The pointwise retention assumption gives an action aH​(s)∈D⁡(s)∩𝒜ε∗​(s)a_{H}(s)\in D(s)\cap\mathcal{A}^{*}_{\varepsilon}(s) at every state. Therefore

maxa∈D⁡(s)⁡Q∗​(s,a)\displaystyle\max_{a\in D(s)}Q^{*}(s,a) ≥Q∗​(s,aH​(s))\displaystyle\geq Q^{*}(s,a_{H}(s))
≥V∗​(s)−ε.\displaystyle\geq V^{*}(s)-\varepsilon.

Together with ΔD​(s)≤Δmax\Delta_{D}(s)\leq\Delta_{\max}, this yields

ΔD​(s)=V∗​(s)−maxa∈D⁡(s)⁡Q∗​(s,a)≤ε0for every ​s.\Delta_{D}(s)=V^{*}(s)-\max_{a\in D(s)}Q^{*}(s,a)\leq\varepsilon_{0}\qquad\text{for every }s.

For the policy πQ\pi_{Q}, the optimal Bellman residual is

bπQ​(s)\displaystyle b_{\pi_{Q}}(s) =V∗​(s)−∑aπQ​(a∣s)​Q∗​(s,a)\displaystyle=V^{*}(s)-\sum_{a}\pi_{Q}(a\mid s)Q^{*}(s,a)
=V∗​(s)−Q∗​(s,aQ​(s))\displaystyle=V^{*}(s)-Q^{*}(s,a_{Q}(s))
=ΔD​(s)\displaystyle=\Delta_{D}(s)
≤ε0.\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon_{0}.

The residual identity derived in the proof of Theorem 3.2 gives

V∗−VπQ=bπQ+γ​PπQ​(V∗−VπQ).V^{*}-V^{\pi_{Q}}=b_{\pi_{Q}}+\gamma P^{\pi_{Q}}(V^{*}-V^{\pi_{Q}}).

Taking sup norms, using ‖bπQ‖∞≤ε0\|b_{\pi_{Q}}\|_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon_{0}, and using that a Markov operator is nonexpansive in the sup norm, we obtain

‖V∗−VπQ‖∞≤ε0+γ​‖V∗−VπQ‖∞.\|V^{*}-V^{\pi_{Q}}\|_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon_{0}+\gamma\|V^{*}-V^{\pi_{Q}}\|_{\infty}.

Rearranging gives

‖V∗−VπQ‖∞≤ε01−γ.\|V^{*}-V^{\pi_{Q}}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\varepsilon_{0}}{1-\gamma}.

By Theorem C.1, the restricted optimal value dominates every supported policy componentwise:

VD∗≥VπQ.V_{D}^{*}\geq V^{\pi_{Q}}.

Also VD∗≤V∗V_{D}^{*}\leq V^{*} because the restricted policy class is a subset of the unrestricted class. Hence, for every state,

0≤V∗​(s)−VD∗​(s)≤V∗​(s)−VπQ​(s)≤ε01−γ.0\leq V^{*}(s)-V_{D}^{*}(s)\leq V^{*}(s)-V^{\pi_{Q}}(s)\leq\frac{\varepsilon_{0}}{1-\gamma}.

This proves (57). ∎

We now replace oracle retention by proxy retention. The key step is to compare any proxy target action with an oracle maximizer through the pairwise fidelity condition.

Proof of Proposition C.8.

Fix a state ss, an action a∈𝒜~ε​(s)a\in\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_{\varepsilon}(s), and a∗​(s)∈arg​maxb⁡Q∗​(s,b)a^{*}(s)\in\argmax_{b}Q^{*}(s,b). Proxy near-optimality implies

Q~​(s,a∗​(s))−Q~​(s,a)\displaystyle\widetilde{Q}(s,a^{*}(s))-\widetilde{Q}(s,a) ≤maxb⁡Q~​(s,b)−Q~​(s,a)\displaystyle\leq\max_{b}\widetilde{Q}(s,b)-\widetilde{Q}(s,a)
≤ε.\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon.

Apply Assumption C.7 to the pair (a∗​(s),a)(a^{*}(s),a):

V∗​(s)−Q∗​(s,a)\displaystyle V^{*}(s)-Q^{*}(s,a) =Q∗​(s,a∗​(s))−Q∗​(s,a)\displaystyle=Q^{*}(s,a^{*}(s))-Q^{*}(s,a)
≤λ⁡[Q~​(s,a∗​(s))−Q~​(s,a)]+δprox\displaystyle\leq\lambda[\widetilde{Q}(s,a^{*}(s))-\widetilde{Q}(s,a)]+\delta_{\mathrm{prox}}
≤λ​ε+δprox.\displaystyle\leq\lambda\varepsilon+\delta_{\mathrm{prox}}.

Thus a∈𝒜λ​ε+δprox∗​(s)a\in\mathcal{A}^{*}_{\lambda\varepsilon+\delta_{\mathrm{prox}}}(s), proving (35). If a set C⁡(s)C(s) intersects the proxy target, an action in that intersection also belongs to the enlarged oracle target. This proves the stated hit-event implication under any state distribution. ∎

Proof of Proposition C.9.

The optimal Bellman identity gives, for every state and action pair,

Q∗​(s,a)−Q∗​(s,b)−[r⁡(s,a)−r⁡(s,b)]\displaystyle Q^{*}(s,a)-Q^{*}(s,b)-[r(s,a)-r(s,b)]
=γ​∑s′[P⁡(s′∣s,a)−P⁡(s′∣s,b)]​V∗​(s′).\displaystyle\quad=\gamma\sum_{s^{\prime}}[P(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)-P(s^{\prime}\mid s,b)]V^{*}(s^{\prime}).

Taking absolute values and then the maximum proves the pairwise condition with λ=1\lambda=1 and δprox=δdyn\delta_{\mathrm{prox}}=\delta_{\mathrm{dyn}}.

For a learned response proxy p^\widehat{p}, add and subtract the immediate-reward difference:

|Q∗​(s,a)−Q∗​(s,b)−[p^​(s,a)−p^​(s,b)]|\displaystyle\left|Q^{*}(s,a)-Q^{*}(s,b)-[\widehat{p}(s,a)-\widehat{p}(s,b)]\right|
≤|Q∗​(s,a)−Q∗​(s,b)−[r⁡(s,a)−r⁡(s,b)]|\displaystyle\quad\leq\left|Q^{*}(s,a)-Q^{*}(s,b)-[r(s,a)-r(s,b)]\right|
+|r⁡(s,a)−p^​(s,a)|+|r⁡(s,b)−p^​(s,b)|\displaystyle\qquad+|r(s,a)-\widehat{p}(s,a)|+|r(s,b)-\widehat{p}(s,b)|
≤δdyn+2​δresp.\displaystyle\quad\leq\delta_{\mathrm{dyn}}+2\delta_{\mathrm{resp}}.

This proves the stated extension.

By Lemma D.2, the range of V∗V^{*} is at most (1−γ)−1(1-\gamma)^{-1}. For any two probability distributions P1,P2P_{1},P_{2} and any function ff with range at most BB,

|𝔼P1​f−𝔼P2​f|≤B​TV⁡(P1,P2).|\mathbb{E}_{P_{1}}f-\mathbb{E}_{P_{2}}f|\leq B\,\operatorname{TV}(P_{1},P_{2}).

Apply this inequality with f=V∗f=V^{*} and B=(1−γ)−1B=(1-\gamma)^{-1}, then maximize over (s,a,b)(s,a,b) and multiply by γ\gamma to obtain (37). ∎

Proxy fidelity controls the filtering term. The next consequence controls the selection term by transferring an approximate critic maximization guarantee to the true optimal action values.

Corollary D.4 (Approximate within-set selection).

Assume D⁡(s)≠∅D(s)\neq\emptyset for every state and let π∈Π⁡(D)\pi\in\Pi(D). Suppose ‖Q^−Q∗‖∞≤δcrit\|\widehat{Q}-Q^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq\delta_{\mathrm{crit}} and the within-set condition (39) holds. Define δ¯sel=𝔼s∼dπ​[δsel​(s)]\overline{\delta}_{\mathrm{sel}}=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\pi}}[\delta_{\mathrm{sel}}(s)]. Then

ζπ,D​(s)≤2​δcrit+δsel​(s).\zeta_{\pi,D}(s)\leq 2\delta_{\mathrm{crit}}+\delta_{\mathrm{sel}}(s). (58)

If (31) also holds, then

V∗​(μ0)−Vπ​(μ0)≤(1−α)​ε0+α​Δmax+2​δcrit+δ¯sel1−γ.V^{*}(\mu_{0})-V^{\pi}(\mu_{0})\leq\frac{(1-\alpha)\varepsilon_{0}+\alpha\Delta_{\max}+2\delta_{\mathrm{crit}}+\overline{\delta}_{\mathrm{sel}}}{1-\gamma}. (59)
Proof of Corollary D.4.

Fix a state ss and abbreviate Ds=D⁡(s)D_{s}=D(s). The uniform critic error implies, for every aa,

Q∗​(s,a)≤Q^​(s,a)+δcritQ^{*}(s,a)\leq\widehat{Q}(s,a)+\delta_{\mathrm{crit}}

and

Q∗​(s,a)≥Q^​(s,a)−δcrit.Q^{*}(s,a)\geq\widehat{Q}(s,a)-\delta_{\mathrm{crit}}.

Taking a maximum in the first inequality gives

maxa∈Ds⁡Q∗​(s,a)≤maxa∈Ds⁡Q^​(s,a)+δcrit.\max_{a\in D_{s}}Q^{*}(s,a)\leq\max_{a\in D_{s}}\widehat{Q}(s,a)+\delta_{\mathrm{crit}}.

Averaging the second inequality under π(⋅∣s)\pi(\cdot\mid s) gives

∑a∈Dsπ⁡(a∣s)​Q∗​(s,a)\displaystyle\sum_{a\in D_{s}}\pi(a\mid s)Q^{*}(s,a) ≥∑a∈Dsπ⁡(a∣s)​[Q^​(s,a)−δcrit]\displaystyle\geq\sum_{a\in D_{s}}\pi(a\mid s)[\widehat{Q}(s,a)-\delta_{\mathrm{crit}}]
=∑a∈Dsπ⁡(a∣s)​Q^​(s,a)−δcrit,\displaystyle=\sum_{a\in D_{s}}\pi(a\mid s)\widehat{Q}(s,a)-\delta_{\mathrm{crit}},

because ∑a∈Dsπ⁡(a∣s)=1\sum_{a\in D_{s}}\pi(a\mid s)=1. Subtracting the second bound from the first yields

ζπ,D​(s)\displaystyle\zeta_{\pi,D}(s) =maxa∈Ds⁡Q∗​(s,a)−∑a∈Dsπ⁡(a∣s)​Q∗​(s,a)\displaystyle=\max_{a\in D_{s}}Q^{*}(s,a)-\sum_{a\in D_{s}}\pi(a\mid s)Q^{*}(s,a)
≤maxa∈Ds⁡Q^​(s,a)−∑a∈Dsπ⁡(a∣s)​Q^​(s,a)+2​δcrit\displaystyle\leq\max_{a\in D_{s}}\widehat{Q}(s,a)-\sum_{a\in D_{s}}\pi(a\mid s)\widehat{Q}(s,a)+2\delta_{\mathrm{crit}}
≤δsel​(s)+2​δcrit.\displaystyle\leq\delta_{\mathrm{sel}}(s)+2\delta_{\mathrm{crit}}.

This proves (58).

Average the statewise inequality under dπd^{\pi}:

ζ¯π,D\displaystyle\overline{\zeta}_{\pi,D} =𝔼s∼dπ​[ζπ,D​(s)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\pi}}[\zeta_{\pi,D}(s)]
≤2​δcrit+𝔼s∼dπ​[δsel​(s)]\displaystyle\leq 2\delta_{\mathrm{crit}}+\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\pi}}[\delta_{\mathrm{sel}}(s)]
=2​δcrit+δ¯sel.\displaystyle=2\delta_{\mathrm{crit}}+\overline{\delta}_{\mathrm{sel}}.

Substituting this bound into Corollary C.5 proves (59). ∎

The combined bound now follows by applying these two transfers in sequence: proxy hits give an enlarged oracle target, and critic and selector errors bound the remaining selection loss.

Proof of Corollary C.10.

Proposition C.8 gives, for every state,

𝒜~ε​(s)⊆𝒜λ​ε+δprox∗​(s).\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_{\varepsilon}(s)\subseteq\mathcal{A}^{*}_{\lambda\varepsilon+\delta_{\mathrm{prox}}}(s).

Therefore the proxy coverage assumption (38) implies

Prs∼dπ⁡(C⁡(s)∩𝒜λ​ε+δprox∗​(s)≠∅)≥1−α.\Pr_{s\sim d^{\pi}}\left(C(s)\cap\mathcal{A}^{*}_{\lambda\varepsilon+\delta_{\mathrm{prox}}}(s)\neq\emptyset\right)\geq 1-\alpha.

Apply Corollary C.5 with the tolerance

ε′=λ​ε+δprox.\varepsilon^{\prime}=\lambda\varepsilon+\delta_{\mathrm{prox}}.

The truncated hit-state loss in that corollary is

min⁡{ε′,Δmax}=εrec.\min\{\varepsilon^{\prime},\Delta_{\max}\}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rec}}.

Thus

V∗​(μ0)−Vπ​(μ0)≤(1−α)​εrec+α​Δmax+ζ¯π,D1−γ.V^{*}(\mu_{0})-V^{\pi}(\mu_{0})\leq\frac{(1-\alpha)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rec}}+\alpha\Delta_{\max}+\overline{\zeta}_{\pi,D}}{1-\gamma}.

Corollary D.4 gives

ζ¯π,D≤2​δcrit+δ¯sel.\overline{\zeta}_{\pi,D}\leq 2\delta_{\mathrm{crit}}+\overline{\delta}_{\mathrm{sel}}.

Substitution proves (41). ∎

For patience, we use the same retention and selection distinction at a single interaction. The collection response is controlled by event inclusion, whereas the response of a selected item also includes the choice error.

Proof of Proposition C.11.

Let

Hp={s:D⁡(s)​ contains an action ​a​ with ​p​(s,a)≥p∗​(s)−ε}.H_{p}=\left\{s:D(s)\text{ contains an action }a\text{ with }p(s,a)\geq p^{*}(s)-\varepsilon\right\}.

Let αp=Prs∼ν⁡(s∉Hp)≤α\alpha_{p}=\Pr_{s\sim\nu}(s\notin H_{p})\leq\alpha.

For every action a∈D⁡(s)a\in D(s), the event {Ya=1}\{Y_{a}=1\} is contained in the union defining pDset​(s)p_{D}^{\mathrm{set}}(s). Hence

pDset​(s)≥maxa∈D⁡(s)⁡p⁡(s,a)p_{D}^{\mathrm{set}}(s)\geq\max_{a\in D(s)}p(s,a)

without any independence assumption. On HpH_{p}, this gives

p∗​(s)−pDset​(s)≤εp.p^{*}(s)-p_{D}^{\mathrm{set}}(s)\leq\varepsilon_{p}.

Outside HpH_{p}, the same difference is at most one. Therefore

𝔼ν​[1−pDset​(s)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[1-p_{D}^{\mathrm{set}}(s)] =𝔼ν​[1−p∗​(s)]+𝔼ν​[p∗​(s)−pDset​(s)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[1-p^{*}(s)]+\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[p^{*}(s)-p_{D}^{\mathrm{set}}(s)]
≤𝔼ν​[1−p∗​(s)]+(1−αp)​εp+αp\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[1-p^{*}(s)]+(1-\alpha_{p})\varepsilon_{p}+\alpha_{p}
≤𝔼ν​[1−p∗​(s)]+(1−α)​εp+α,\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[1-p^{*}(s)]+(1-\alpha)\varepsilon_{p}+\alpha,

where the last inequality uses εp≤1\varepsilon_{p}\leq 1.

For the pre-response item selector,

p∗​(s)−pD,κitem​(s)\displaystyle p^{*}(s)-p_{D,\kappa}^{\mathrm{item}}(s) =p∗​(s)−maxa∈D⁡(s)⁡p⁡(s,a)+δselp​(s).\displaystyle=p^{*}(s)-\max_{a\in D(s)}p(s,a)+\delta_{\mathrm{sel}}^{p}(s).

The first term is at most εp\varepsilon_{p} on HpH_{p} and at most one outside HpH_{p}. Taking expectations gives

𝔼ν​[p∗​(s)−pD,κitem​(s)]≤(1−α)​εp+α+δ¯selp,\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[p^{*}(s)-p_{D,\kappa}^{\mathrm{item}}(s)]\leq(1-\alpha)\varepsilon_{p}+\alpha+\overline{\delta}_{\mathrm{sel}}^{p},

which proves (43).

For either mechanism, denote its positive-response probability by pmech​(s)p_{\mathrm{mech}}(s). Its expected patience decrease is

c+​pmech​(s)+c−​[1−pmech​(s)]=c++(c−−c+)​[1−pmech​(s)].c_{+}p_{\mathrm{mech}}(s)+c_{-}[1-p_{\mathrm{mech}}(s)]=c_{+}+(c_{-}-c_{+})[1-p_{\mathrm{mech}}(s)].

The best single item replaces pmech​(s)p_{\mathrm{mech}}(s) by p∗​(s)p^{*}(s). Subtracting and applying the corresponding no-response bound proves (44) and (45). ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.3.

The proof combines a finite horizon performance identity with separate bounds for filtering and selection. Unlike the stationary argument, it conditions on the information available at each stage, so the policy and critic may change during the session.

By the finite-horizon Bellman equation and the controlled Markov property,

Qh∗​(sh,ah)\displaystyle Q_{h}^{*}(s_{h},a_{h}) =rh(sh,ah)+𝔼[Vh+1∗(sh+1)∣ℋh,ah],\displaystyle=r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})+\mathbb{E}\!\left[V_{h+1}^{*}(s_{h+1})\mid\mathcal{H}_{h},a_{h}\right],
𝔼[Rh∣ℋh,ah]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[R_{h}\mid\mathcal{H}_{h},a_{h}] =rh​(sh,ah).\displaystyle=r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h}).

The tower property therefore gives

𝔼⁡[Vh∗​(sh)−Qh∗​(sh,ah)]=𝔼⁡[Vh∗​(sh)−Rh−Vh+1∗​(sh+1)].\mathbb{E}\!\left[V_{h}^{*}(s_{h})-Q_{h}^{*}(s_{h},a_{h})\right]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[V_{h}^{*}(s_{h})-R_{h}-V_{h+1}^{*}(s_{h+1})\right].

Summing from h=1h=1 to HH, using s1∼μ0s_{1}\sim\mu_{0} and VH+1∗=0V_{H+1}^{*}=0, yields

V1∗​(μ0)−V1RLCP​(μ0)=∑h=1H𝔼⁡[Vh∗​(sh)−Qh∗​(sh,ah)].V_{1}^{*}(\mu_{0})-V_{1}^{\mathrm{RLCP}}(\mu_{0})=\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}\!\left[V_{h}^{*}(s_{h})-Q_{h}^{*}(s_{h},a_{h})\right]. (60)

For each stage, split the optimal action gap into the loss from the execution set and the loss from the selected action:

Δh\displaystyle\Delta_{h} =Vh∗​(sh)−maxa∈Dh⁡Qh∗​(sh,a),\displaystyle=V_{h}^{*}(s_{h})-\max_{a\in D_{h}}Q_{h}^{*}(s_{h},a),
ζh\displaystyle\zeta_{h} =maxa∈Dh⁡Qh∗​(sh,a)−Qh∗​(sh,ah).\displaystyle=\max_{a\in D_{h}}Q_{h}^{*}(s_{h},a)-Q_{h}^{*}(s_{h},a_{h}).

Because DhD_{h} is nonempty and ah∈Dha_{h}\in D_{h} almost surely, both gaps are nonnegative, Δh≤ΔHmax\Delta_{h}\leq\Delta_{H}^{\max}, and

Vh∗​(sh)−Qh∗​(sh,ah)=Δh+ζh.V_{h}^{*}(s_{h})-Q_{h}^{*}(s_{h},a_{h})=\Delta_{h}+\zeta_{h}.

Suppose first that ehK=0e_{h}^{K}=0. Choose bh∈ChK∩𝒜~ε,h​(sh)b_{h}\in C_{h}^{K}\cap\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_{\varepsilon,h}(s_{h}) and ah∗∈arg​maxa∈𝒜⁡Qh∗​(sh,a)a_{h}^{*}\in\argmax_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{h}^{*}(s_{h},a). Membership of bhb_{h} in the proxy target implies

Q~h​(sh,ah∗)−Q~h​(sh,bh)≤maxa∈𝒜⁡Q~h​(sh,a)−Q~h​(sh,bh)≤ε.\widetilde{Q}_{h}(s_{h},a_{h}^{*})-\widetilde{Q}_{h}(s_{h},b_{h})\leq\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\widetilde{Q}_{h}(s_{h},a)-\widetilde{Q}_{h}(s_{h},b_{h})\leq\varepsilon.

Applying (47) to (ah∗,bh)(a_{h}^{*},b_{h}) gives

Vh∗​(sh)−Qh∗​(sh,bh)\displaystyle V_{h}^{*}(s_{h})-Q_{h}^{*}(s_{h},b_{h}) =Qh∗​(sh,ah∗)−Qh∗​(sh,bh)\displaystyle=Q_{h}^{*}(s_{h},a_{h}^{*})-Q_{h}^{*}(s_{h},b_{h})
≤λ⁡(Q~h​(sh,ah∗)−Q~h​(sh,bh))+δprox\displaystyle\leq\lambda\bigl(\widetilde{Q}_{h}(s_{h},a_{h}^{*})-\widetilde{Q}_{h}(s_{h},b_{h})\bigr)+\delta_{\mathrm{prox}}
≤λ​ε+δprox.\displaystyle\leq\lambda\varepsilon+\delta_{\mathrm{prox}}.

Since bh∈ChK⊆Dhb_{h}\in C_{h}^{K}\subseteq D_{h}, this proves Δh≤εH\Delta_{h}\leq\varepsilon_{H} on {ehK=0}\{e_{h}^{K}=0\}. On {ehK=1}\{e_{h}^{K}=1\}, the universal bound Δh≤ΔHmax\Delta_{h}\leq\Delta_{H}^{\max} applies. Hence, pathwise,

Δh≤εH+(ΔHmax−εH)​ehK.\Delta_{h}\leq\varepsilon_{H}+(\Delta_{H}^{\max}-\varepsilon_{H})e_{h}^{K}. (61)

By definition, a capped miss is either a raw miss or a raw hit removed by the cap, and these events are disjoint. Thus

ehK=e~h+hhK.e_{h}^{K}=\widetilde{e}_{h}+h_{h}^{K}.

The recursion (46) has exactly the form required by Theorem 3.1. Since the step sizes are positive and nonincreasing and W~H≤W\widetilde{W}_{H}\leq W, that theorem gives, almost surely,

1H​∑h=1He~h≤α+W+η1ηH​H.\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\widetilde{e}_{h}\leq\alpha+\frac{W+\eta_{1}}{\eta_{H}H}.

Consequently,

1H​∑h=1HehK≤α+W+η1ηH​H+1H​∑h=1HhhK.\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}e_{h}^{K}\leq\alpha+\frac{W+\eta_{1}}{\eta_{H}H}+\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}h_{h}^{K}.

Average (61) over stages and then take expectations. This yields

1H​∑h=1H𝔼⁡[Δh]≤\displaystyle\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{h}]\leq{} (1−α)​εH+α​ΔHmax\displaystyle(1-\alpha)\varepsilon_{H}+\alpha\Delta_{H}^{\max} (62)
+(ΔHmax−εH)​(W+η1ηH​H+h¯HK).\displaystyle+(\Delta_{H}^{\max}-\varepsilon_{H})\left(\frac{W+\eta_{1}}{\eta_{H}H}+\overline{h}_{H}^{K}\right).

The remaining term is the gap between the best retained action and the action actually selected. Since DhD_{h} and Q^h\widehat{Q}_{h} are ℋh\mathcal{H}_{h} measurable, the critic condition implies

maxa∈Dh⁡Qh∗​(sh,a)\displaystyle\max_{a\in D_{h}}Q_{h}^{*}(s_{h},a) ≤maxa∈Dh⁡Q^h​(sh,a)+δcrit,\displaystyle\leq\max_{a\in D_{h}}\widehat{Q}_{h}(s_{h},a)+\delta_{\mathrm{crit}},
𝔼⁡[Qh∗​(sh,ah)∣ℋh]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[Q_{h}^{*}(s_{h},a_{h})\mid\mathcal{H}_{h}\right] ≥𝔼⁡[Q^h​(sh,ah)∣ℋh]−δcrit.\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}\!\left[\widehat{Q}_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})\mid\mathcal{H}_{h}\right]-\delta_{\mathrm{crit}}.

Subtracting the second inequality from the first and using (49) gives

𝔼⁡[ζh∣ℋh]≤2​δcrit+δsel,h.\mathbb{E}[\zeta_{h}\mid\mathcal{H}_{h}]\leq 2\delta_{\mathrm{crit}}+\delta_{\mathrm{sel},h}.

The assumed integrability permits taking expectations. Averaging over stages gives

1H​∑h=1H𝔼⁡[ζh]≤2​δcrit+δ¯sel,H.\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}[\zeta_{h}]\leq 2\delta_{\mathrm{crit}}+\overline{\delta}_{\mathrm{sel},H}. (63)

Finally, the filtering and selection bounds control the two components of each gap in (60). Substituting (62) and (63), using Δh+ζh\Delta_{h}+\zeta_{h}, and multiplying by HH gives (19). No step requires the policy, critic, or threshold to converge; the argument uses their stated stagewise information and error conditions. ∎

D.6 Proof of Greedy Preservation and Conditional Recovery

We first show that thresholding, capping, and fallback all preserve the same critic maximizer. We then use that preservation to express policy loss through pairwise critic error and the remaining selection gap.

Proof of Proposition C.13.

Fix tt and ss, and let a^t​(s)\widehat{a}_{t}(s) be the first maximizer of Q^t​(s,⋅)\widehat{Q}_{t}(s,\cdot) under the fixed action order. Every score gt​(s,a)g_{t}(s,a) is nonnegative, and gt​(s,a^t​(s))=0g_{t}(s,\widehat{a}_{t}(s))=0. If τt<0\tau_{t}<0, the raw set is empty and the minimum score fallback is exactly a^t​(s)\widehat{a}_{t}(s). If τt≥0\tau_{t}\geq 0, the raw set contains every critic maximizer. Its first action in increasing score order is a^t​(s)\widehat{a}_{t}(s), so every cap with Kt≥1K_{t}\geq 1 retains this action. In both cases,

a^t​(s)∈Dt​(s),maxa∈Dt​(s)⁡Q^t​(s,a)=maxa⁡Q^t​(s,a).\widehat{a}_{t}(s)\in D_{t}(s),\qquad\max_{a\in D_{t}(s)}\widehat{Q}_{t}(s,a)=\max_{a}\widehat{Q}_{t}(s,a).

Thus the execution set preserves the global critic maximizer selected by the fixed action order. A greedy selector using that order consequently returns the same item with or without filtering.

Choose any a∗​(s)∈arg​maxa⁡Q∗​(s,a)a^{*}(s)\in\argmax_{a}Q^{*}(s,a). Substituting Q∗=Q^t−ξtQ^{*}=\widehat{Q}_{t}-\xi_{t} into the optimal Bellman residual gives

bπt​(s)\displaystyle b_{\pi_{t}}(s) =Q∗​(s,a∗​(s))−∑aπt​(a∣s)​Q∗​(s,a)\displaystyle=Q^{*}(s,a^{*}(s))-\sum_{a}\pi_{t}(a\mid s)Q^{*}(s,a)
=Q^t​(s,a∗​(s))−∑aπt​(a∣s)​Q^t​(s,a)\displaystyle=\widehat{Q}_{t}(s,a^{*}(s))-\sum_{a}\pi_{t}(a\mid s)\widehat{Q}_{t}(s,a)
+∑aπt(a∣s)[ξt(s,a)−ξt(s,a∗(s))].\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{a}\pi_{t}(a\mid s)\bigl[\xi_{t}(s,a)-\xi_{t}(s,a^{*}(s))\bigr].

For the first difference, replace Q^t​(s,a∗​(s))\widehat{Q}_{t}(s,a^{*}(s)) by its maximum over all actions, which equals its maximum over Dt​(s)D_{t}(s) by the preceding argument. This upper bounds that difference by σt​(s)\sigma_{t}(s). Every bracket in the final sum is at most βt\beta_{t}, and the policy weights are nonnegative and sum to one. Consequently,

0≤bπt​(s)≤σt​(s)+βt.0\leq b_{\pi_{t}}(s)\leq\sigma_{t}(s)+\beta_{t}.

The residual identity in the proof of Theorem 3.2 now gives

V∗​(μ0)−Vπt​(μ0)\displaystyle V^{*}(\mu_{0})-V^{\pi_{t}}(\mu_{0}) =11−γ​𝔼s∼dπt​[bπt​(s)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\pi_{t}}}[b_{\pi_{t}}(s)]
≤σ¯t+βt1−γ.\displaystyle\leq\frac{\overline{\sigma}_{t}+\beta_{t}}{1-\gamma}.

For every state and action pair, the triangle inequality gives

|ξt​(s,a)−ξt​(s,b)|≤|ξt​(s,a)|+|ξt​(s,b)|≤2​‖Q^t−Q∗‖∞.|\xi_{t}(s,a)-\xi_{t}(s,b)|\leq|\xi_{t}(s,a)|+|\xi_{t}(s,b)|\leq 2\|\widehat{Q}_{t}-Q^{*}\|_{\infty}.

Maximizing shows that βt≤2​‖Q^t−Q∗‖∞\beta_{t}\leq 2\|\widehat{Q}_{t}-Q^{*}\|_{\infty}.

Suppose a strictly suboptimal state and action pair exists. Finiteness makes the minimum of its positive gaps strictly positive, so Δmin>0\Delta_{\min}>0 is well defined. Let a^∈arg​maxa⁡Q^t​(s,a)\widehat{a}\in\argmax_{a}\widehat{Q}_{t}(s,a). Then

V∗​(s)−Q∗​(s,a^)\displaystyle V^{*}(s)-Q^{*}(s,\widehat{a}) =Q^t​(s,a∗​(s))−Q^t​(s,a^)\displaystyle=\widehat{Q}_{t}(s,a^{*}(s))-\widehat{Q}_{t}(s,\widehat{a})
+ξt​(s,a^)−ξt​(s,a∗​(s))\displaystyle\quad+\xi_{t}(s,\widehat{a})-\xi_{t}(s,a^{*}(s))
≤βt,\displaystyle\leq\beta_{t},

because the first difference is nonpositive. If a^\widehat{a} were suboptimal and βt<Δmin\beta_{t}<\Delta_{\min}, this would imply

Δmin≤V∗​(s)−Q∗​(s,a^)≤βt<Δmin,\Delta_{\min}\leq V^{*}(s)-Q^{*}(s,\widehat{a})\leq\beta_{t}<\Delta_{\min},

a contradiction. This proves ranking consistency for every state. Since Dt​(s)D_{t}(s) contains a global critic maximizer, every critic maximizer within Dt​(s)D_{t}(s) is also a global critic maximizer. A policy supported on these actions is therefore supported on the true optimal actions. Lemma D.1 proves its optimality. If no strictly suboptimal pair exists, every policy is supported on optimal actions, and the same lemma applies directly.

Finally, the quantitative value convergence statement follows by taking limits in the value bound above. For exact greedy selection, βt→0\beta_{t}\to 0 implies βt<Δmin\beta_{t}<\Delta_{\min} at every sufficiently large index when a positive gap exists. At those indices the policy is optimal. A unique optimal action at each state forces the action distribution to be the same point mass at all such indices. If several actions are optimal, support on those actions imposes no requirement that the distribution converge. None of these steps uses convergence of a parameter vector or of the threshold. ∎

Appendix E Experiment Details

This appendix describes the comparison methods and the reported metrics. The metric definitions distinguish utility, catalog exposure, and retained set size so that the numerical comparisons can be interpreted separately from the calibration guarantee.

E.1 Baseline Details

  • •

    A2C: an advantage actor–critic method that updates the policy using advantage-weighted policy gradients and trains the critic to estimate the state-value function (Mnih et al., 2016).

  • •

    DDPG: an off-policy deterministic actor–critic algorithm designed for continuous action spaces, which is applied to continuous action representations for slate recommendation (Lillicrap et al., 2016).

  • •

    TD3: an extension of DDPG that mitigates value overestimation and improves training stability through clipped double Q-learning, delayed policy updates, and target policy smoothing (Fujimoto et al., 2018).

  • •

    HAC: a hyper-actor–critic method that represents recommendation slates in a latent action space and decomposes slate generation into hyper-action inference and effect-action selection (Liu et al., 2023).

E.2 Evaluation Metrics

The metrics below describe complete simulated sessions. Let NN be the number of evaluated sessions, TnT_{n} the length of session nn, and Rn,tR_{n,t} its reward at request tt. Let Ln,tL_{n,t} denote the item collection used by the evaluation code at that request. A baseline with fixed slate size has |Ln,t|=M|L_{n,t}|=M, while the reported RLCP set size uses its retained execution collection. Catalog diversity and ILD require the evaluated collection to be defined consistently across methods.

Depth.

We first measure how long the interaction continues. Depth is the mean number of recommendation steps before departure:

Depth=1N​∑n=1NTn.\mathrm{Depth}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}T_{n}.

A larger value means that the simulated sessions contain more interactions; it does not specify how much reward those interactions produce.

Average Reward.

To measure the reward per interaction while giving equal weight to each session, we first average within sessions and then across sessions:

AvgReward=1N​∑n=1N1Tn​∑t=1TnRn,t.\mathrm{AvgReward}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1}{T_{n}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{n}}R_{n,t}.

Total Reward.

In contrast, total reward records the cumulative reward of a session before averaging across sessions:

TotalReward=1N​∑n=1N∑t=1TnRn,t.\mathrm{TotalReward}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{n}}R_{n,t}.

Diversity.

To measure exposure across users, catalog diversity counts distinct items in the BB active requests of an evaluation batch and averages this count over HevalH_{\mathrm{eval}} evaluation steps, following KuaiSim:

Diversity=1Heval​∑h=1Heval|⋃j=1BLj,h|.\mathrm{Diversity}=\frac{1}{H_{\mathrm{eval}}}\sum_{h=1}^{H_{\mathrm{eval}}}\left|\bigcup_{j=1}^{B}L_{j,h}\right|.

The tables call this metric Diversity. It counts exposed items and is distinct from the proxy retention probability controlled by calibration.

Intra List Diversity.

Catalog diversity does not describe how similar the items within a request are. ILD measures that separate property through mean pairwise dissimilarity within each evaluated collection. Write Mn,t=|Ln,t|M_{n,t}=|L_{n,t}| and let eae_{a} be the embedding of item aa. Then

ILD\displaystyle\mathrm{ILD} =1∑n=1NTn​∑n=1N∑t=1Tn2Mn,t​(Mn,t−1)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sum_{n=1}^{N}T_{n}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{n}}\frac{2}{M_{n,t}(M_{n,t}-1)}
×∑1≤j<k≤Mn,td⁡(e(Ln,t)j,e(Ln,t)k).\displaystyle\quad\times\sum_{1\leq j<k\leq M_{n,t}}d\!\left(e_{(L_{n,t})_{j}},e_{(L_{n,t})_{k}}\right).

Here d⁡(⋅,⋅)d(\cdot,\cdot) is the item dissimilarity function and Mn,tM_{n,t} is the number of items in the evaluated collection at request tt of session nn. For Mn,t=1M_{n,t}=1, the corresponding diversity term is defined as zero.

Admissible Set Size.

Finally, the average admissible set size records how many items remain after filtering, averaged over evaluation requests:

SetSize=1∑n=1NTn​∑n=1N∑t=1Tn|Ln,t|.\mathrm{SetSize}=\frac{1}{\sum_{n=1}^{N}T_{n}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{n}}|L_{n,t}|.

A smaller value indicates that fewer alternatives are retained. It is not a measure of total computation, since it excludes scoring the candidate pool and obtaining the proxy label.
